titleStmt.title: Subliminal priming with nearly perfect performance in the prime-classification task

bibl.title: Subliminal priming with nearly perfect performance in the prime-classification task

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Thus, we conclude that subliminal priming effects can be observed even when taking the steps necessary to guard against the task-difficulty artifact.

span.label: subliminal priming
span.quote: A subliminal priming effect is obtained when undetectable prime stimuli modulate targetrelated processes in some way.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: To address the concerns with Pratte and Rouder’s (2009) procedure for controlling task difficulty, the primes in the present experiment were presented in color (red or green) in both the targetand prime-classification tasks.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: using a backward mask that is visually similar to the prime (a letter string masking a letter-string prime) suppresses prime identity strongly enough to reach chance-level identification at durations that still produce priming, whereas dissimilar and repeated masks let the prime pop out
span.quote: This decision, along with their use of identical forward and backward masks, which causes the prime to “pop out” or appear in relief, contributed to the lack of effective masking in their experiment.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: differences in masking procedure, rather than differences in control of task difficulty, are what drive the opposite conclusions of the two studies
span.quote: We suggest that our findings stand in contrast to those of Pratte and Rouder (2009) because of important differences in the masking procedures between the two studies.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: when primes and targets share a stimulus set, learned stimulus-response mappings can be triggered automatically by an unseen prime, so apparent above-chance prime classification may reflect nonconscious motor activation rather than awareness
span.quote: then above-chance performance in the prime-classification task may index nonconsciously elicited motor processes— not visual awareness.

span.label: Even with 240 prime-classification trials the design remains open to the low-power criticism levelled at subliminal priming studies.
span.quote: But the present study, despite including 1.5 times as many trials in the prime-classification task (N = 240) as the targetclassification task (N = 160), is still susceptible to the criticism that Rouder, Morey, and colleagues have persuasively leveled against many subliminal priming studies (cf. Morey, Rouder, & Speckman, 2008, 2009; Rouder, Morey, Speckman, & Pratte, 2007).

span.label: The prime-classification measure used here may itself have been insufficiently sensitive to prime awareness.
span.quote: The third possibility, which is related to the second, is that the prime-classification measure in the present experiment may not have been sufficiently sensitive.

span.label: The .95 posterior criterion used to declare subliminality may be too strict, and the priming result is also reported under a relaxed .90 criterion.
span.quote: It should be noted that the criterion of .95 is very strict, and may be too strict for this application (Jeff Rouder, personal communication).

span.label: subliminal priming
span.quote: If, in a separate task that assesses prime awareness, subjects are not able to identify the prime stimuli at better than chance levels (i.e., d′ is not statistically different from zero), then subliminal priming is said to have occurred

span.label: prime-classification task
span.quote: In a recent critique of subliminal priming, Pratte and Rouder (Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, 71, 1276–1283, 2009) suggested that previous claims of subliminal priming may have been due to a failure to control the task difficulty between the experiment proper and the prime-classification task

span.label: task difficulty
span.quote: In a recent critique of subliminal priming, Pratte and Rouder (Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, 71, 1276–1283, 2009) suggested that previous claims of subliminal priming may have been due to a failure to control the task difficulty between the experiment proper and the prime-classification task

span.label: task-difficulty artifact
span.quote: To guard against this potential “task-difficulty artifact,” some researchers have included long-duration primes in the prime-classification task

span.label: **THE CRITERION STATED AS AN IF-THEN, WHICH IS WORTH HOLDING VERBATIM:** `If, in a separate task that assesses PRIME AWARENESS, subjects are not able to identify the prime stimuli at BETTER THAN CHANCE levels (i.e., d' is not statistically different from zero), then SUBLIMINAL PRIMING IS SAID TO HAVE OCCURRED.` **`is said to have occurred`** - the phenomenon is the conjunction of two measurements, and the paper is explicit that the word is licensed by the second one. dehaene1998 and holcomb2005 argue about WHAT was processed without awareness; this record is about what licenses the word `subliminal` at all, which is the prior question and the corpus had no clean statement of it
span.quote: If, in a separate task that assesses prime awareness, subjects are not able to identify the prime stimuli at better than chance levels (i.e., d′ is not statistically different from zero), then subliminal priming is said to have occurred

span.label: **AND THE CRITIQUE IT ANSWERS IS AN ATTACK ON THE MEASUREMENT, NOT ON THE EFFECT:** `In a recent critique of subliminal priming, Pratte and Rouder (2009) suggested that previous claims of subliminal priming may have been due to A FAILURE TO CONTROL THE TASK DIFFICULTY between the experiment proper and the prime-classification task.` **If the certifying task is simply harder, chance performance on it certifies nothing.** That is the strongest form of methodological criticism - it does not dispute a result, it disputes what the result is evidence OF - and a corpus that records priming findings without recording this cannot represent why the literature is contested
span.quote: In a recent critique of subliminal priming, Pratte and Rouder (Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, 71, 1276–1283, 2009) suggested that previous claims of subliminal priming may have been due to a failure to control the task difficulty between the experiment proper and the prime-classification task

span.label: **THE ANSWER IS BUILT INTO THE STIMULUS RATHER THAN ARGUED IN A DISCUSSION - PRINT THE PRIMES IN COLOUR:** `In the prime-classification task, subjects reported the color of the primes VERY ACCURATELY, indicating ALMOST PERFECT CONTROL OF TASK DIFFICULTY, but they COULD NOT IDENTIFY the primes.` 92.1% on colour, chance on identity, **same stimulus, same trial, within subject.** The colour report proves the task was easy and the subject was attending, so the identity failure cannot be blamed on difficulty. **A control made of the stimulus, not of an argument** - and the cleanest reply to an artifact objection I have tagged
span.quote: In the prime-classification task, subjects reported the color of the primes very accurately, indicating almost perfect control of task difficulty, but they could not identify the primes

span.label: **AND A FOOTNOTE CARRIES THE STRONGEST SENTENCE IN THE PAPER:** `The primes that were presented for 40 to ~60 ms were VISIBLE (d' > 2.0); the primes presented for LESS THAN 40 ms were NOT VISIBLE (d' not different from zero), AND YET THEY PRODUCED RELIABLE PRIMING EFFECTS.` **Visible primes prime and invisible primes prime.** So the priming function and the awareness function are separable, and a study that finds priming has learned nothing about awareness until it measures awareness separately - which is the whole argument of this paper, stated in a footnote about a different experiment
span.quote: The primes that were presented for 40 to ~60 ms were visible (d′ > 2.0); the primes presented for less than 40 ms were not visible (d′ not different from zero), and yet they produced reliable priming effects

span.label: contradicts → Pratte and Rouder (2009)
span.quote: But Pratte and Rouder’s conclusion that controlling for the task-difficulty artifact eliminates subliminal priming lacks empirical support.

span.label: contradicts → Pratte and Rouder (2009)
span.quote: We suggest that our findings stand in contrast to those of Pratte and Rouder (2009) because of important differences in the masking procedures between the two studies.

span.label: replicates → Finkbeiner & Forster (2008); Kouider & Dehaene (2007)
span.quote: These results (see Fig. 3a) replicate several findings reported in the literature (cf. Finkbeiner & Forster, 2008; Kouider & Dehaene, 2007, for reviews), although this is the first demonstration of masked congruence priming that we are aware of with distinctly colored prime stimuli.

span.label: builds-on → Morey et al. (2008) mass-at-chance (MAC) model
span.quote: The prime-classification data from the present experiment were analyzed using the one-parameter MAC model (Morey et al., 2008), which is available as a package for the R language (http://r-forge.r-project.org/projects/massatchance/).

span.label: subliminal priming —operationalised-as→ prime-classification task
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — **THE CLAIM IS ONLY AS GOOD AS THE TASK, AND THAT IS WHY THE CRITIQUE LANDS.** `Subliminal` is not a property the experimenter sets by choosing 40 ms; it is conferred by chance performance on this second task. Weight 0.95 - the paper's own framing sentence, and the whole design follows from it. The quote is Pratte and Rouder's criticism rather than Finkbeiner's definition, which is deliberate: the operationalisation is clearest in the sentence that attacks it.
span.quote: In a recent critique of subliminal priming, Pratte and Rouder (Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, 71, 1276–1283, 2009) suggested that previous claims of subliminal priming may have been due to a failure to control the task difficulty between the experiment proper and the prime-classification task

span.label: task difficulty —causes→ subliminal priming
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.85 — **THIS EDGE IS SOMEONE ELSE'S CLAIM, RECORDED BECAUSE THIS PAPER EXISTS TO REFUTE IT.** Pratte and Rouder argue that uncontrolled task difficulty produces APPARENT subliminality - `previous claims ... may have been DUE TO a failure to control the task difficulty` - so the arrow runs from the confound to the reported phenomenon, and `increases` means more uncontrolled difficulty yields more spurious claims. **Read it with the `distinct-from` edge below, which is Finkbeiner's answer**: control the difficulty and the effect is still there. Weight 0.85, and the `may have been` hedge is inside the quote. A corpus that recorded only the refutation would leave a reader wondering what was being refuted.
span.quote: In a recent critique of subliminal priming, Pratte and Rouder (Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, 71, 1276–1283, 2009) suggested that previous claims of subliminal priming may have been due to a failure to control the task difficulty between the experiment proper and the prime-classification task

span.label: subliminal priming —distinct-from→ task-difficulty artifact
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — **THE RESULT, AND `distinct-from` IS DOING REAL WORK HERE.** The artifact was proposed as an ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATION of subliminal priming; this record separates them by controlling the artifact and keeping the effect. So the edge records not that two concepts differ, but that one was offered as the other and failed. Weight 0.9 rather than 0.95 because the paper itself attributes the contrast with Pratte and Rouder to `important differences in the masking procedures between the two studies` - which is a second unresolved difference between the labs, stated by the author.
span.quote: Thus, we conclude that subliminal priming effects can be observed even when taking the steps necessary to guard against the task-difficulty artifact

span.label: repeated-measures ANOVA
span.quote: A 2 (prime duration: 40 vs. 50 ms) × 2 (prime type: congruent vs. incongruent) repeated measures ANOVA was conducted

span.label: one-sample t-test
span.quote: To establish whether primeclassification accuracy rates differed from chance, we first used a traditional one-sample t test.

span.label: paired-samples t-test
span.quote: Following Rouder et al. (2007), the RTs for the 17 subjectby-prime-duration combinations for which subliminality was confirmed were entered into a paired-samples t test (twotailed) to determine whether subliminal priming had occurred.

span.label: Bayes factor
span.quote: the evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis, we used the Bayes factor calculator (Rouder, Speckman, Sun, Morey, & Iverson, 2009).

span.label: hierarchical Bayesian model
span.quote: have introduced a hierarchical model within the Bayesian framework that offers researchers a way to resolve the null-sensitivity problem.

span.label: posterior probability
span.quote: If this posterior probability is above some criterion, say .95, then that individual is judged to be performing at chance.

span.label: null-hypothesis significance testing
span.quote: Merikle and Reingold have argued against using standard null-hypothesis significance testing (NHST) in the study of subliminal perception

span.label: signal-detection sensitivity (d-prime)
span.quote: With 40-ms primes, the mean accuracy rate was 51.8% (d′ = 0.098; one-sample t test: t(20) = 1.67, p = .19), and with 50-ms primes it was 55.6% (d′ = 0.308; one-sample t test: t(20) = 2.43, p = .02).

span.label: LOESS local regression
span.quote: As is clear from the fitted polynomial (LOESS), the magnitude of the priming effect does not decrease as the criterion for subliminality increases.

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: Error bars represent 95% confidence intervals

span.label: Reliable masked congruence priming was obtained at both 40 ms and 50 ms prime durations.
span.quote: The planned comparisons revealed significant priming effects with both 40-ms primes [t(20) = 2.5, p < .05] and 50-ms primes [t(20) = 2.2, p < .05].

span.label: Presenting primes in colour let subjects report the prime's colour almost as accurately as they classified targets, which the author takes as successful equating of difficulty across the two tasks.
span.quote: These high accuracy scores, which approximate the accuracy scores in the target-classification task, indicate near-perfect control of task difficulty.

span.label: Even though colour was reported near ceiling, prime identity could not be identified above chance at 40 ms, while identity identification did exceed chance at 50 ms.
span.quote: With 40-ms primes, the mean accuracy rate was 51.8% (d′ = 0.098; one-sample t test: t(20) = 1.67, p = .19), and with 50-ms primes it was 55.6% (d′ = 0.308; one-sample t test: t(20) = 2.43, p = .02).

span.label: A Bayesian mass-at-chance analysis confirmed genuine subliminality for most subjects at 40 ms but almost none at 50 ms.
span.quote: As is clear, subliminality was confirmed for only 1 subject in the condition with 50-ms primes. In contrast, 16 of the 21 subjects were judged to be at chance with the 40-ms primes.

span.label: Restricting the priming analysis to only those subject-by-duration cells whose subliminality was confirmed still yielded a significant priming effect.
span.quote: The results of this t test indicated a significant subliminal priming effect [t(16) = 2.79, p = .01].

span.label: The size of the priming effect did not shrink as the evidence for subliminality got stronger, arguing that the priming is not carried by partially visible primes.
span.quote: As is clear from the fitted polynomial (LOESS), the magnitude of the priming effect does not decrease as the criterion for subliminality increases.

span.label: The study therefore rejects Pratte and Rouder's claim that controlling the task-difficulty artifact eliminates subliminal priming.
span.quote: Thus, we conclude that subliminal priming effects can be observed even when taking the steps necessary to guard against the task-difficulty artifact.

span.label: subliminal priming effect
span.quote: A subliminal priming effect is obtained when undetectable prime stimuli modulate targetrelated processes in some way.

span.label: target-classification task
span.quote: Following Pratte and Rouder, I will refer to this first task as the target-classification task.

span.label: task-difficulty artifact
span.quote: To guard against this potential “task-difficulty artifact,” some researchers have included long-duration primes in the prime-classification task.

span.label: mass-at-chance (MAC) model
span.quote: The MAC model assumes that each subject’s performance reflects a true latent ability score that, like a z score, varies both positively and negatively.

span.label: null-sensitivity problem
span.quote: This is the null-sensitivity problem, and trying to resolve it through the addition of more and more trials is not practical for most researchers, not to mention for their subjects.

span.label: prime duration (40 vs 50 ms)
span.quote: The prime was presented for either 40 or 50 ms, followed by the backward mask for 10 or 20 ms (fixing prime–target SOA at 60 ms) and then the target stimulus for 300 ms.

span.label: prime type (congruent vs incongruent)
span.quote: In each block, each target stimulus (N = 10) was rotated through each of the eight design cells that were formed by crossing the factors Prime Color (green and red), Prime Duration (40 and 50 ms), and Prime Type (congruent and incongruent).

span.label: presenting the primes in colour in both tasks (task-difficulty manipulation)
span.term: presenting the primes in colour in both tasks (task-difficulty manipulation)
span.quote: the primes in the present experiment were presented in color (red or green) in both the targetand prime-classification tasks

span.label: response time to the target
span.quote: Incorrect responses (3.5%) were excluded from the RT analyses, as were trials with RTs below 100 ms (< 0.1%).

span.label: prime colour accuracy and prime identity accuracy
span.term: prime colour accuracy and prime identity accuracy
span.quote: With 40-ms primes, the mean accuracy rate was 51.8% (d′ = 0.098; one-sample t test: t(20) = 1.67, p = .19), and with 50-ms primes it was 55.6% (d′ = 0.308; one-sample t test: t(20) = 2.43, p = .02).

span.label: prime colour (red/green) as a balancing dummy factor
span.term: prime colour (red/green) as a balancing dummy factor
span.quote: Prime Color was a dummy factor that was included only to balance the number of red and green primes across the experimental conditions equally.

span.label: prime-target SOA held constant at 60 ms
span.term: prime-target SOA held constant at 60 ms
span.quote: The prime was presented for either 40 or 50 ms, followed by the backward mask for 10 or 20 ms (fixing prime–target SOA at 60 ms) and then the target stimulus for 300 ms.

span.label: M = 92.1% — mean accuracy of reporting the prime's colour in the prime-classification task
span.quote: since subjects were highly successful in reporting the prime’s color (M = 92.1%)

span.label: both greater than 90% — colour-report accuracy and target-classification accuracy, showing the two tasks were matched for difficulty
span.quote: the accuracy rates are approximately equal to those in the target-classification task (both greater than 90%)

span.label: 51.8% ... 55.6% — prime identity accuracy at 40 ms and at 50 ms prime durations
span.quote: With 40-ms primes, the mean accuracy rate was 51.8% (d′ = 0.098; one-sample t test: t(20) = 1.67, p = .19), and with 50-ms primes it was 55.6% (d′ = 0.308; one-sample t test: t(20) = 2.43, p = .02).

span.label: 16 of the 21 — subjects judged to be performing at chance on prime identity with 40-ms primes by the MAC model
span.quote: As is clear, subliminality was confirmed for only 1 subject in the condition with 50-ms primes. In contrast, 16 of the 21 subjects were judged to be at chance with the 40-ms primes.

span.label: 21 — number of participants in the experiment
span.quote: Twenty-one undergraduate psychology students participated for course credit.

span.label: Bayes factor of 0.26 — Bayes factor for the priming effect among subliminality-confirmed cells, i.e. the alternative is 3.85 times more likely than the null
span.quote: In this case, the sample size of 17 and a t value of 2.79 yield a Bayes factor of 0.26.

span.label: 9:1 ... 16:1 — odds in favour of subliminality and the resulting odds in favour of priming under the relaxed .90 criterion
span.quote: Thus, with 9:1 odds in favor of subliminality, this experiment yielded 16:1 odds in favor of priming.

span.label: approximately 570 — prime-classification trials that would be needed, at n = 21 and 52% true performance, to keep the chance of wrongly accepting the null below 5%
span.quote: For example, with a sample size of 21 and a mean true performance of 52%, one would need approximately 570 prime-classification trials to bring the probability of wrongly accepting the null hypothesis down
